Deplete

dih-PLEET · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To deplete to use up the supply of something until little or none is left.

Decades of overfishing had depleted the coral reef's fish population so badly that entire species disappeared from local waters.

Worked Example

By the final mile of the marathon, the runner's glycogen stores were completely depleted, leaving her legs heavy and slow.

Nothing was stolen or broken -- the runner's body had simply used up its fuel supply, exactly what deplete describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

exhaust: to use up completely

drain: to gradually empty a supply of something

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

replenish: to fill something up again

restore: to bring something back to its original level or condition

Where it sits · how much of the supply is gone — reduce → deplete → empty

reduce vs. deplete: To reduce a supply is to make it smaller, a milder change than deplete.

empty vs. deplete: To empty a supply completely is to leave absolutely nothing behind, an even more total loss than deplete.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: down, away (Latin)

Root — plete

Root — plete: to fill (from Latin plere, 'to fill' -- the same root as in complete)

Put it together

Put it together: Deplete combines de- ('down, away') with plete (from Latin plere, 'to fill') -- it's almost the reverse of complete (com- + plere, 'to fill fully'). To deplete something is literally to 'un-fill' it.

Use the root in a new word: complete

Use the root in a new word: complete: The puzzle wasn't complete until the very last piece clicked into place.

Root Check

Word Choice

Deplete describes using up a supply of something concrete, like energy, money, fuel, or natural resources -- compare it to desiccate, which more often describes something (like enthusiasm) drained of feeling rather than a physical supply.
